subject: ela
intro: Reading fluency means reading accurately, at a good pace, and with expression. A fluent reader does not read one word at a time like a robot. Instead, they group words into phrases, speed up and slow down at the right places, and change their voice to match punctuation and feeling. Fluent reading helps you understand what you read because your brain has energy left over to think about meaning.

items.prompt:
A student read 'The dog ran fast.' as 'The. Dog. Ran. Fast.' — pausing after every single word. What does this tell you about their fluency?
A) They read too slowly, word-by-word, without phrasing
B) They read too fast
C) They read with good expression

steps: A fluent reader groups words together into meaningful phrases, not individual words.
Reading 'The. Dog. Ran. Fast.' with a pause after every word is called word-by-word reading.
Word-by-word reading is too slow and choppy — it makes it hard to understand the meaning.
A fluent reader would say 'The dog ran fast.' as one smooth phrase.
solution.answer: A) They read too slowly, word-by-word, without phrasing. Fluent reading means grouping words together smoothly.

items.prompt:
Which sentence would a fluent reader say with rising intonation (voice going up at the end)?
A) It is raining.
B) Is it raining?

steps: Intonation means the rise and fall of your voice.
A period (.) signals the end of a statement — the voice falls or stays flat.
A question mark (?) signals a question — the voice typically rises at the end.
'It is raining.' is a statement: voice goes down at the end.
'Is it raining?' is a question: voice goes UP at the end.
solution.answer: B) Is it raining? A question mark signals rising intonation — the voice goes up at the end.

items.prompt:
A student reads the sentence 'Watch out!' in a flat, quiet voice. What is wrong with their expression?
A) Nothing — flat is always correct
B) The exclamation point signals excitement or urgency; they should read it with a louder, more energetic voice
C) They should read it even more slowly

steps: Punctuation gives clues about how to read with expression.
An exclamation point (!) signals strong feeling: excitement, surprise, urgency, or fear.
Reading 'Watch out!' in a flat voice ignores the punctuation cue.
A fluent reader adjusts their voice to match the punctuation — louder and more urgent for an exclamation point.
solution.answer: B) The exclamation point signals excitement or urgency. A fluent reader reads 'Watch out!' with a louder, more energetic voice.

items.prompt:
A student reads a sentence and realizes a word does not make sense. She goes back and rereads the sentence. This is an example of:
A) Skipping a hard word
B) Self-correcting to confirm word recognition and understanding
C) Reading too slowly on purpose

steps: Good readers monitor themselves — they notice when something does not make sense.
When a word or sentence does not make sense, a fluent reader goes back and rereads.
Rereading to fix a mistake is called self-correcting.
Self-correction helps confirm that the reader understood what the text said.
solution.answer: B) Self-correcting to confirm word recognition and understanding. Going back to reread when something seems wrong is a key fluency skill.

items.prompt:
A student is about to read a passage for the first time. She notices the title is 'Amazing Ocean Animals'. Before she reads, she thinks about what she knows about ocean animals. How does this help her fluency?
A) It does not help fluency at all
B) Reading with purpose and prior knowledge helps her recognize words faster and understand what she reads
C) It will make her read every word too carefully

steps: Reading with purpose means having a reason or goal before you start reading.
When a reader thinks about what they already know about a topic, their brain is 'warmed up'.
This helps them recognize topic-related words more quickly.
Faster word recognition allows the reader to focus on meaning — which is the goal of fluency.
solution.answer: B) Reading with purpose and prior knowledge helps her recognize words faster and understand what she reads. Fluency supports comprehension.

items.prompt:
A student reads: 'She smiled, / waved at her friend, / and walked home.' The slashes show where she paused. Is this good phrasing?
A) No — she should pause after every word
B) Yes — she paused at natural phrase boundaries, making the reading smooth and meaningful
C) No — she should never pause
items.hint: Think about where it is natural to pause when you speak. Commas often mark natural phrase boundaries.

steps: Fluent readers pause at natural phrase boundaries, not after every word.
Commas and other punctuation signal where to pause.
The student paused after 'smiled,' and 'friend,' — both are comma-marked boundaries.
This grouping into phrases makes the reading smooth and easier to understand.
solution.answer: B) Yes. Pausing at phrase boundaries (often marked by commas) is a sign of fluent, expressive reading.

items.prompt:
A student reads the same passage three times. Each time, he reads it more smoothly and makes fewer mistakes. What does this tell us about repeated reading?
A) Repeated reading does not improve fluency
B) Repeated reading builds fluency — accuracy, rate, and expression improve with practice
C) He should only read new passages, never the same one twice
items.hint: Think about why practicing anything over and over helps you get better at it.

steps: Fluency improves with practice, just like any other skill.
The first reading is often rough — the reader is figuring out unknown words.
Each re-reading allows the reader to focus more on expression and phrasing.
Repeated reading is a proven strategy for building reading rate and accuracy.
solution.answer: B) Repeated reading builds fluency. Each time through, accuracy, rate, and expression all improve.

items.prompt:
A teacher notices a student reads very fast but makes many mistakes and cannot answer questions afterward. What part of fluency needs the most work?
A) Rate — she needs to read even faster
B) Accuracy — reading too fast with many errors hurts comprehension
C) Expression — she needs more excitement in her voice
items.hint: Fluency has three parts: accuracy, rate, and expression. Which one is causing the problem here?

steps: The student reads fast but makes many errors and cannot comprehend the text.
Fluency requires ACCURACY (reading words correctly), not just speed.
Reading fast without accuracy means the brain is not processing the actual words.
When accuracy drops, comprehension drops too.
She needs to slow down and read words correctly, not race through the text.
solution.answer: B) Accuracy needs the most work. Reading with too many errors, even at a fast rate, hurts comprehension. Accurate reading must come before speed.

items.prompt:
A student reads dialogue: '"Run!" shouted the boy.' How should a fluent reader read the word 'Run!'?
A) In a soft, slow voice
B) In a loud, urgent voice because the exclamation point and the word 'shouted' signal strong emotion
C) In a flat, even voice
items.hint: Look at two clues: the punctuation inside the quotation marks and the word that tells how the character spoke.

steps: Two clues signal how to read this word: the exclamation point (!) and the word 'shouted'.
An exclamation point signals strong feeling or urgency.
The word 'shouted' tells us the character is speaking loudly.
A fluent reader reads 'Run!' in a loud, urgent voice to match both clues.
solution.answer: B) Loud and urgent. Both the exclamation point and the word 'shouted' tell the reader to use a strong, loud voice.

items.prompt:
A student reads: 'The big, fuzzy caterpillar slowly climbed the tall oak tree.' She reads it as one continuous stream without any pauses. What should she do?
A) Add pauses at the commas and after long phrases to improve phrasing
B) Read it even faster with no pauses
C) Read it backwards to check for mistakes
items.hint: Look for punctuation cues. The comma tells you where a natural pause belongs.

steps: The comma after 'big' and 'fuzzy' signals a natural pause in reading.
Even without commas, long phrases should be grouped meaningfully.
Reading with natural pauses helps listeners (and the reader) understand the meaning.
She should pause after 'big, fuzzy caterpillar' and read the rest as a smooth phrase.
solution.answer: A) Add pauses at the commas and after long phrases. Phrasing — grouping words into meaningful chunks — is a key part of fluent, expressive reading.
